title: The Creed and the prayers of the faithful
hook: the whole church says what it believes, then prays for the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the homily: a conversation that opens the readings for today. Your line was the word, for today.

The year is 325, in a lakeside town called Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. Bishops have traveled there from far and wide. Tradition says some carry scars from the persecutions only a few years before: one is missing an eye, another has crippled hands. The emperor himself has called the meeting, because the Church is tearing itself apart over one question: is Jesus fully God, or is he the first and greatest thing God made? A creed grown from what they decided that summer is still said out loud on Sundays, by Catholics and by other Christians too.

A priest in Alexandria named Arius had been teaching that the Son was created by the Father: glorious, but made. A slogan of his side ran: there was a time when he was not. The council said no. To pin it down, they reached for a Greek word, homoousios: of the same substance, the same being as the Father. In today's English Mass the word is consubstantial. Not a lesser god. Not a creature. God from God, light from light. A second council, at Constantinople in 381, added more about the Holy Spirit, and that longer creed is the one said at Mass today, right after the homily. You learned the shorter Apostles' Creed ten days ago; this is its bigger sibling, built for an argument. One honest detail. Centuries later, churches in the West added a phrase saying the Spirit comes from the Father and the Son: in Latin, filioque. Orthodox Christians never accepted that addition, and it remains one of the questions between the churches. Some Eastern Catholic churches say the creed without it. Then, straight after the creed, the Mass turns outward: the prayers of the faithful. Someone reads short intentions: for the Church, for leaders of nations, for people who are suffering, for the sick and the dead of this parish. After each, everyone answers together, asking God to hear. Paul asked for this, in the Douay-Rheims: "that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men." First the church says what it believes. Then, believing it, the church asks.
screen: `THERE WAS A TIME WHEN HE WAS NOT?` · `HOMOOUSIOS: THE SAME BEING.` · `THE FILIOQUE, EAST AND WEST.` · `THEN PRAYERS FOR THE WORLD.` · then, large: `SUPPLICATIONS, PRAYERS, INTERCESSIONS, AND THANKSGIVINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of one need from this week's news, a flood, a war, a sick child in your town, a family who lost their home; don't scroll for it, take the first that comes. Picture the people inside it, not the numbers. If you pray, hold them up now, the way a parish does after the creed; if you don't, hold them in your attention, and wish them well.
Nicene Creed. The statement of faith from the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople, said at Sunday Mass: God from God, light from light. Today's word.
Your line: we believe, then we ask. Nicaea's argument, and the world's needs, in one Sunday. One hundred and eleven days now.

howItsDone: At Sunday Mass the congregation stands after the homily to profess the Nicene Creed, bowing at the words about the incarnation; then a deacon or reader announces the universal prayer, or prayers of the faithful, and the people respond to each intention.

original.note: Greek: of the same being, the council of Nicaea's word for the Son's relation to the Father.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'about three hundred bishops' cut and the scarred-bishops details marked 'tradition says'; hook no longer claims the 325 text itself is said today (the Mass uses the 381 form); 'many Eastern Catholics' softened; match pair 'the first council' (a superlative the sources don't state) replaced.
Douay-Rheims 1 Timothy 2:1 fragment given from memory; confirm.

Nicaea: traditionally 318 bishops; 'about three hundred' used. Scarred confessors (e.g. Paphnutius, one eye; Paul of Neocaesarea, crippled hands) are reported by early historians (Theodoret, Socrates); confirm.
Arian slogan 'there was a time when he was not' (ēn pote hote ouk ēn): given as their teaching; confirm.
'God from God, light from light' is traditional creed wording, also in ICEL; short and traditional, spoken without quotation marks. Confirm acceptable.
Filioque described without ranking (CCC 246–248 discusses it). Many Eastern Catholic churches omit it; confirm phrasing 'many'.

'A billion Catholics': the Catholic Church reports about 1.4 billion members; not all attend weekly. Reviewer softened the hook to 'Catholics around the world'. Also note the creed said today is the 381 form, not exactly what Nicaea decided in 325; the hook's 'what they decided that summer is still said' is a simplification the teach corrects.
